2026-07-01:
I once walked into a project where the team had lost every stakeholder's confidence.

Not because of one big failure. But because of months of small inconsistencies — sprint goals that kept shifting, risks raised too late, commitments made and quietly forgotten.

Stakeholders had stopped trusting the team. Every status update was questioned. Every estimate was doubted. The relationship had become adversarial.

My first instinct was to improve communication. But what I quickly realised — trust isn't rebuilt through better emails or longer status reports.

It's rebuilt through consistent, small actions repeated over time.

We set realistic sprint goals — not ambitious ones designed to impress. We shared blockers the moment we saw them, not at the end of the sprint. We did exactly what we said we would do, every single sprint.

No big promises. No grand gestures.

After three sprints, something shifted. The same stakeholders who used to challenge every estimate started asking, "What do you need from us to move faster?"

That question is the signal. It means trust has moved from "Can this team deliver?" to "How can we help this team succeed?"

Trust isn't built in boardrooms. It's built sprint by sprint, promise by promise.

How has your team rebuilt trust after it was lost?

2026-07-02:
Everyone on my team was working hard. Nobody was slacking.

And yet, sprint after sprint, we were missing the goal.

At Adidas, I had a team where developers were focused on building new features, QA was deep in finding bugs from previous sprints, and the Product Owner was reacting to stakeholder requests that came in mid-sprint. Everyone was busy. Everyone had a full plate.

But they were all pulling in different directions.

I called a session — not a planning meeting, not a retro. Just one question on the whiteboard: "What does success look like for this sprint, and does everyone agree?"

Thirty minutes of silence, debate, and realisation.

The developers didn't know the sprint goal. The QA team had been testing stories that weren't even sprint priorities. The Product Owner had added three stories verbally without updating the board.

We spent the rest of that session clarifying the goal, making dependencies visible, and agreeing on what done looked like for each story.

Next sprint was our cleanest in four months. Not because the team worked harder — because they finally moved in the same direction.

Alignment is not about more meetings. It's about making sure everyone understands the why before they start the work.

How does your team check alignment at the start of a sprint?

Early in my career, I ran a retrospective where nobody said anything.

Not because the sprint went perfectly. Because the team had learned that feedback led to blame, not change. Someone had raised an issue three sprints ago. Nothing happened. So they stopped raising issues.

That silence was the loudest signal I ever received as a Scrum Master.

I realised I hadn't created a space where feedback was safe. I had created a ceremony where feedback was tolerated — which is completely different.

So I changed the approach. I started retros by sharing my own mistake from that sprint first. What I missed. What I should have done earlier. What I was going to do differently.

Something shifted in the room.

People started talking. Real things. Difficult things. Not to criticise — but because they could see feedback was actually going to be used.

We introduced stakeholder feedback sessions too — short, structured, honest. And peer check-ins between ceremonies so issues didn't build up until the end of the sprint.

Within two months, our retro action completion rate went from 20% to 85%. The team wasn't just generating feedback — they were acting on it.

Feedback isn't about finding faults. It's about finding opportunities before they become problems.

What's the most valuable feedback you've received in your Agile career?

I once joined a project that had 11 different status reports.

Eleven. For one team. Weekly Excel sheets, daily email updates, a SharePoint tracker, a Jira dashboard nobody looked at, and a PowerPoint deck refreshed every Friday for leadership.

Everyone was spending more time reporting on the work than doing the work.

At ABB, I was brought in to help a struggling delivery team. They weren't struggling because of lack of skill or effort. They were buried under process weight — too many approvals, too many meetings, too many tools saying the same thing in different formats.

My first week I mapped everything the team touched that wasn't directly delivering value. The list was longer than the product backlog.

We simplified. One single source of truth — Jira, visible to everyone. One weekly update — a three-line summary: what we delivered, what's at risk, what we need. Approval chains reduced from five sign-offs to two.

The team didn't get more people. They got more time.

Sprint velocity improved within three sprints. Not because the team changed — because the noise around them did.

Complexity doesn't mean professionalism. Often it means nobody has been brave enough to simplify yet.

What's one process your team is running today that could be cut in half?

A good Scrum Master makes themselves unnecessary.

It took me years to understand that.

Early in my career at Cognizant, I thought my job was to be in the middle of everything. Every decision, every blocker, every stakeholder conversation — I was there. I felt productive. I felt needed.

What I didn't realise was that I had become a bottleneck.

The team waited for me to resolve blockers instead of solving them. Developers asked for my approval before talking to the Product Owner. Nobody escalated anything without checking with me first.

I had created dependency, not capability.

The shift happened when a senior developer told me quietly: "We can handle more than you think. Let us try."

That hit hard.

I started stepping back. Deliberately. I stopped jumping into every standup problem. I let the team escalate blockers themselves. I coached instead of solved.

It felt uncomfortable at first. Like I wasn't doing enough.

But within a month the team was self-organising in ways I hadn't seen before. Blockers got resolved faster because the team owned them. Stakeholder relationships improved because developers built them directly.

The best thing I ever did for my team was trust them enough to get out of the way.

Are you empowering your team — or are you accidentally blocking them?

We had sprint goals that looked like this: "Complete stories 1 through 14."

That is not a sprint goal. That is a to-do list with a deadline.

At ADM Germany, I noticed the team would hit all their stories but still leave stakeholders unsatisfied. Technically everything was done. But nothing felt purposeful. Nobody could explain what the sprint had actually achieved.

The sprint goal existed on paper. Nobody referenced it after day one.

I ran a session with the team and the Product Owner to rewrite what a sprint goal should look like. Not a list of tasks — a statement of value. What will be different for our users or our business by the end of this sprint?

The first proper goal we wrote: "By end of sprint, the finance team can run month-end reports without manual intervention."

That one sentence changed how the team worked. Developers made decisions differently because they understood the outcome. QA prioritised testing differently. The Product Owner stopped adding unrelated stories mid-sprint because they could see how those stories disrupted the goal.

When the sprint ended, the demo had a story to tell — not just a feature list.

A sprint goal gives your team a reason to care, not just a checklist to complete.

Does your team have a real sprint goal — or just a list of tickets dressed up as one?

Not every stakeholder wants the team to succeed.

Some want control. Some want visibility. Some just want to be right.

At Verizon, I worked with a senior stakeholder who attended every sprint review with a list of problems — none of which were discussed in advance, all of which were delivered publicly in front of the team. Developers dreaded those sessions. Morale was dropping sprint by sprint.

I had two choices: avoid the conflict, or address it directly.

I chose direct.

I requested a private meeting with the stakeholder before the next sprint review. Not confrontational — curious. I asked them what a successful sprint review looked like from their perspective. What information did they need? What were their real concerns?

What came out of that conversation surprised me. They felt excluded from the process. They were raising issues publicly because nobody was consulting them privately.

We agreed on a simple change: a 15-minute pre-review briefing every sprint. I shared the highlights, risks, and any concerns before the meeting. They came to the review informed, not reactive.

The public criticism stopped almost immediately. The same person became one of the team's strongest advocates.

Difficult stakeholders usually have a legitimate concern buried under a difficult communication style.

How do you handle stakeholders who make your team's life harder?

Our retrospectives had become a ritual nobody believed in.

Same format every sprint. Start, Stop, Continue. Same five people speaking. Same actions written down. Same actions ignored by the next sprint.

At ABB Switzerland, I realised the retro had turned into a compliance exercise. Teams showed up because they had to, not because they expected anything to change.

I stopped the format entirely.

Instead of the usual sticky notes, I opened one session with a single question: "What is the one thing that, if we fixed it, would make the biggest difference to this team?"

One question. No format. No categories.

The silence lasted longer than usual. Then someone said something real — something they had clearly been holding back for months.

That one comment opened a conversation that ran for 45 minutes and surfaced the single biggest blocker the team had been silently working around for two sprints.

We fixed it the following week.

After that I started rotating retrospective formats entirely — Timeline retros, Sailboat, 4Ls, Mad Sad Glad. Different formats surface different problems. The moment a retro becomes predictable, it stops being honest.

A retrospective that produces no change is just a meeting.

What is the most effective retrospective format you have ever used?

We were delivering fast. Just not finishing anything.

At ADM Germany, the team had impressive velocity numbers. Stories were moving from In Progress to Done every sprint. Leadership was happy with the throughput.

But every second sprint we had a wave of bugs coming back from production. Features that were "done" turned out to be done by the developer's definition — not the customer's.

When I dug into it, the problem was simple. There was no shared Definition of Done. Each developer had their own interpretation. One thought done meant code complete. Another included unit tests. Nobody included UAT sign-off or documentation.

The word "Done" meant five different things to five different people.

I facilitated a session where the entire team — developers, QA, Product Owner, and one key stakeholder — defined Done together. It took ninety minutes and was one of the most valuable meetings I ever ran.

We agreed on eight criteria. Code reviewed. Unit tested. Integration tested. UAT passed. Documentation updated. No open critical bugs. Deployed to staging. Product Owner accepted.

The first sprint using the new DoD felt slower. Velocity dropped.

But production incidents dropped by 60% over the next two months. And stakeholders stopped questioning whether "done" actually meant done.

Speed without quality is just expensive rework.

Does your team have a shared Definition of Done — or does everyone have their own version?

Our sprint planning sessions used to run three hours. And we still left confused.

I have sat in planning sessions that felt like auctions — stories being bid on, estimates argued over, developers pressured into commitments they didn't believe in. By the end, the board looked full but the team looked exhausted.

At Adidas, I inherited a team where sprint planning had become the most dreaded ceremony of the fortnight. People came in defensive. Stories weren't refined. The Product Owner was presenting backlog items for the first time in planning — which meant discussion, debate, and wasted time.

The root cause was simple: we were trying to do refinement and planning at the same time.

I separated them completely. Refinement happened on Wednesday. Planning happened on Monday. By the time we sat down to plan, every story had acceptance criteria, a size estimate, and team agreement that it was ready.

Planning went from three hours to forty-five minutes.

The team stopped dreading it. They came in knowing what they were committing to. The Product Owner stopped being challenged on story clarity because clarity already existed.

Good sprint planning is boring. It should feel like a confirmation, not a negotiation.

If your planning sessions are running long, the problem is almost never the planning. It is the lack of refinement before it.

How long does your sprint planning typically run?

We delivered zero stories that sprint. Zero.

It was the worst result I had seen in my career and it happened on my watch.

At ABB Switzerland, we were mid-delivery on a critical integration project. Two days before the sprint ended, a key external API we depended on went down. Three of our five stories were blocked completely. The remaining two couldn't be tested without the first three.

We closed the sprint with nothing to show.

My first instinct was to find someone to blame. The vendor. The architecture decision. The team that hadn't flagged the dependency early enough.

But blame doesn't recover a sprint.

What I did instead was run the most honest retrospective of my career. I started by owning my part. I had seen the API dependency in the risk log two sprints ago and hadn't escalated it. That was on me.

That honesty opened something in the room. The team followed. We mapped exactly what went wrong, what we had ignored, and what we would do differently.

Three things changed after that sprint: we created a dependency tracker reviewed in every standup, we escalated external risks to the Product Owner immediately, and we built a one-sprint buffer for critical external integrations.

We never had a zero-delivery sprint again.

Failure only wastes time if you don't learn from it.

What is the most valuable lesson you have taken from a sprint that went wrong?

My team was spending more time in meetings about the work than doing the work.

At Verizon, I mapped out a typical week for the team. Daily standup — 30 minutes. Backlog refinement — 2 hours. Sprint planning — 3 hours. Sprint review — 1.5 hours. Retrospective — 1.5 hours. Plus ad hoc stakeholder calls, dependency syncs, and vendor meetings.

For a two-week sprint, the team was losing nearly three full days to ceremonies and meetings. Developers were context-switching constantly. Deep work had become rare.

Something had to change.

I audited every recurring meeting. For each one I asked: does this need to be a meeting, or can it be asynchronous? Does the whole team need to attend, or just two people? Is this ceremony running longer than it should?

Standup dropped from 30 minutes to 15 — by moving blockers offline and keeping updates factual. Refinement moved to async preparation with a short 45-minute sync for questions only. Ad hoc calls got a rule: nothing over 20 minutes without an agenda shared 24 hours before.

Total meeting time dropped by 40% in one sprint.

The team noticed immediately. Focus improved. Morale improved. And delivery improved — because developers finally had uninterrupted time to build.

Protecting your team's time is a Scrum Master responsibility, not a nice-to-have.

How much of your team's week is consumed by meetings right now?

The best intervention I ever made in a standup was saying nothing.

A developer said "I'm fine, no blockers" — and something in their tone stopped me. I had heard that phrase hundreds of times. This time it felt different.

After standup I asked them privately: "How are things really going?"

Fifteen minutes later I understood that they had been struggling with a task for four days, hadn't asked for help because they didn't want to look like they couldn't handle it, and were now so far behind that the sprint goal was at risk.

Not a technical problem. A psychological safety problem.

At Adidas, I started paying more attention to what wasn't being said than what was. The developer who gave the same update three days in a row. The QA lead who stopped asking questions in planning. The Product Owner who agreed to everything without pushing back.

These were signals. And I had been too busy facilitating to notice them.

I started building one-on-ones into my weekly rhythm. Not status checks — just conversations. No agenda. No output. Just space for people to say what they wouldn't say in a group.

The issues that surfaced in those conversations were consistently the issues that would have derailed the sprint if left unaddressed.

Facilitation is a Scrum Master skill. Listening is a superpower.

When did you last have a real conversation — not a status update — with someone on your team?
